objectives: Name the common shapes and say what they look like.
Name the common colours and find them around you.
Use the new shape and colour words in a sentence.
Tell the difference between a circle and an oval.
Hunt for shapes and colours in your home and outside.
Make a picture of your own with shapes and colours.

sections.body:
A **shape** is the outside of a thing. A **colour** is how that thing looks.

Shapes are everywhere. The moon is round, so it has a **circle**. A door is straight and has four corners, so it has a **rectangle**. The roof of a house has a point at the top, so it has a **triangle**.

Colours are everywhere too. The sky is **blue**. Grass is **green**. A ripe mango is **yellow** and a tomato is **red**.

When you learn shapes and colours, you can describe anything in the world. You can tell your friend which cup you want, or draw a house on paper.

Children like shapes because they are a game. You can look for a circle, then a square, then a triangle. There is always another one to find.
examples: I want the red cup, please.
sections.heading: What are shapes and colours?

sections.body:
Here are the shapes you will use the most.

A **circle** is round. It has no corners. A wheel, a coin and a plate are circles.

A **square** has four equal sides and four sharp corners. A cracker and a floor tile are squares.

A **triangle** has three sides and three corners. A roof, a slice of pizza and a road sign are triangles.

A **rectangle** has four sides and four corners, but it is longer than it is wide. A door, a book and a phone are rectangles.

An **oval** is like a circle that has been stretched. An egg and a rugby ball are ovals.

A **star** has points. It is the shape of the stars in the sky at night.

A **heart** has two round bumps on top and a point at the bottom.

Many real things have more than one shape. A cup is a cylinder, and a cylinder has two flat circles at the ends.
sections.heading: The shapes we see every day

sections.body:
Colours are easier to see when you name them one by one.

**Red** is the colour of fire, of a tomato and of a red envelope for Lunar New Year.

**Blue** is the colour of the sky and the sea.

**Yellow** is the colour of the sun, of a banana and of a school bus.

**Green** is the colour of grass and leaves.

**Orange** is the colour of an orange fruit. It is also a colour, not only a fruit.

**Purple** is the colour of grapes and of a violet flower.

**Brown** is the colour of wood, of soil and of chocolate.

**Black** is the colour of night and of a dark night sky.

**White** is the colour of snow, of milk and of clean paper.

Some things have two colour words. The sea can be **blue** and **green** at the same time. Light green is called **light green**, and deep green is called **dark green**. When you say the full name, people know exactly what you mean.
sections.heading: The colours around us

sections.body:
These are the words you need to talk about shapes and colours.

A **circle** is a round shape with no corners.

A **square** has four equal sides and four corners.

A **triangle** has three sides and three corners.

A **rectangle** has four sides and four corners, and it is longer than it is wide.

**Red** is the colour of fire and of a ripe tomato.

**Blue** is the colour of the sky on a clear day.

Say each word out loud. Then point to something in the room that has that shape or that colour.
examples: I can see a circle in the window.
Find something blue in the room.

A shape with four sides and four corners. It is longer than it is wide. A book is a rectangle.
The colour of fire, of a ripe tomato and of a red envelope.

sections.body:
Shape hunting is a game you can play anywhere. Here is how to play it well.

First, choose one shape to look for. Say it out loud, like "circle".

Next, walk slowly and look around. Check the things near you. On the table, on the floor, on the wall.

Then, say the colour too. "A red circle!" or "a yellow rectangle!" Now you are finding two things at once.

After that, change the shape. Try to find a triangle before you find a square.

At the end, name your favourite find. Tell someone else about it.

If you play with a friend, the game is to find the same thing first. But look properly. Speed is fun, but looking properly is the real skill.
examples: I am looking for a circle.
Now I am hunting for a triangle.
sections.heading: How to hunt for shapes and colours
steps: Choose one shape to look for.
Walk slowly and look at the things near you.
Say the colour of what you find.
Change to a new shape and keep looking.
Tell someone else your favourite find.

sections.body:
You can draw any picture with simple shapes. This is how artists start too.

A **house** is a square with a triangle on top. A **sun** is a yellow circle. A **tree** is a brown rectangle with a green circle on top.

A **robot** is made of squares and rectangles. A **flower** is a circle in the middle with long thin shapes around it.

You can cut shapes from coloured paper and glue them down. You can use a shape sorter box. You can build with blocks.

When you make something, say the shapes as you work: a big blue square, and a small yellow circle.

Then look at your picture from far away. Does it still look like what you wanted? If not, add one more shape and try again.
examples: I draw a house from a square and a triangle.
The sun is a yellow circle.
I glue the shapes onto the paper.
sections.heading: Making pictures with shapes and colours

item.summary: Everything around you has a shape and a colour. After reading this, you can name the common shapes and colours, find them in your home and your street, and use them to draw and build your own pictures.
item.title: Learning About Shapes and Colors
